elements.quote: Conclusions: Non-pharmacological interventions can be effective in addressing depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The provided abstract text is explicitly from a systematic review/meta-analysis and is framed as a review (the “Objective…”, “We included randomized controlled trials…”, “Conclusions” wording in the abstract corresponds to a systematic review).

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract contains an explicit objective/review question statement.

elements.quote: Study Selection: We included randomized controlled trials comparing non-pharmacological interventions to control conditions for depressive symptoms in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The abstract provides explicit inclusion criteria (RCTs, non-pharmacological interventions vs control, depressive symptoms after stroke).

elements.quote: Data Sources: A literature search was performed through the following databases from January 2000 to August 2018: MEDLINE; CINAHL Plus; Scopus; Academic Search Complete; Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials; Scopus; and Library, Information Science and Technology Abstracts.
elements.reason: The abstract names information sources/databases and provides the search date range (used to indicate when sources were last searched).
No method for assessing risk of bias in included studies is reported in the provided abstract text.

elements.quote: Data Synthesis: Thirteen non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into four types: complementary and alternative therapy (five trials, 228 participants), exercise (four trials, 263 participants), psychosocial therapy (two trials, 216 participants), and multifactorial therapy (two trials, 358 participants).
elements.reason: The abstract describes how results were categorized/synthesized, but it does not explicitly report the full methods used to assess risk of bias or the specific statistical meta-analysis approach (e.g., model type, effect size computations) within the abstract text provided.

elements.quote: Of 1703 identified articles, 22 trials were included in narrative synthesis, of which 13 were eligible for meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (22 trials in narrative synthesis; 13 for meta-analysis).

elements.quote: Data Synthesis: Thirteen non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into four types: complementary and alternative therapy (five trials, 228 participants), exercise (four trials, 263 participants), psychosocial therapy (two trials, 216 participants), and multifactorial therapy (two trials, 358 participants).
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes relevant study characteristics including participant counts by intervention type.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes (post-intervention and follow-up), including effect estimates with 95% CIs.

elements.quote: Overall beneficial effects of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms were found both post-intervention (effect size [ES] = -0.24, 95% confidence Interval [CI]: -0.37 to -0.11, p < 0.05) and at follow-up (ES = -0.22, CI: -0.36 to -0.07, p < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract reports summary effect estimates (ES) with confidence intervals for the meta-analytic main outcomes.
The abstract summarizes overall effects and does not explicitly describe separate between-group comparisons with the direction of effect favoring a specific group.
The abstract provided does not report limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: Conclusions: Non-pharmacological interventions can be effective in addressing depressive symptoms in people after stroke. Complementary and alternative therapy and psychosocial therapy appear to be promising strategies for improving post-stroke depressive symptoms. Future studies are required to identify a personalized approach for people with specific conditions such as cognitive impairment.
elements.reason: The abstract provides general interpretation of results and implications for practice/future research.
No primary source of funding is reported in the provided abstract text.
No study register name or registration number is reported in the provided abstract text.

elements.quote: Prevalence of major depression in people after stroke is 25% at the acute stage and 31% at 3 months poststroke 2 ; however, few individuals receive effective management for depressive symptoms post-stroke. 3 Unaddressed depressive symptoms can lead to devastating effects; not only do they stunt progress in therapy, but they can also negatively affect stroke outcomes, with increased morbidity, mortality, and poorer functional recovery. 4 Previous studies have been conducted to identify appropriate interventions for post-stroke depression; two common types are pharmacological interventions and non-pharmacological interventions (NPIs). 5-9 Three meta-analyses have been conducted to provide synthesized evidence on the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for depressive symptoms following stroke, but results were mixed. 5,6,9 ... Moreover, it is recognized that the application of pharmacological interventions might be further limited due to adverse effects, long response times, potential medication adverse events, and low adherence rates. 8,10,11 ... Currently, an abundance of evidence supports the effectiveness of NPIs for depression in other clinical populations. 10,13 Three reviews have identified several NPIs for post-stroke depression and have qualitatively provided evidence. 8,11,14
elements.reason: The introduction describes the current state of knowledge on depression after stroke, existing evidence for pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, and points to uncertainties/mixed results (e.g., pharmacological meta-analyses mixed; qualitative rather than quantitative NPI reviews).

elements.quote: Therefore, to address this research gap, this study aimed to conduct a meta-analysis to synthesize and compare the available evidence regarding the effectiveness of various NPIs for treating depression in people following stroke.
elements.reason: The importance/need for the review is explained as addressing a research gap (lack of quantitative demonstration of effectiveness across NPI types) and synthesizing/comparing available evidence.

elements.quote: Three reviews have identified several NPIs for post-stroke depression and have qualitatively provided evidence. 8,11,14 In particular, the latest review indicated that therapies demonstrating a reduction in depressive symptoms include problem-solving therapy, acupuncture, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, music therapy, exercise, light therapy, motivational interviewing, and robotic-assisted therapy. 8 However, none of these reviews quantitatively demonstrated the effectiveness of different types of NPIs.
elements.reason: The manuscript discusses prior reviews and explicitly explains why a new review is needed (existing reviews are qualitative and do not quantitatively demonstrate effectiveness of different NPI types).
No evidence provided describes a proposed mechanism of action of the interventions.
No evidence provided considers a logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes for complex interventions/delivery contexts.

elements.quote: Objective: To compare the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions on depressive symptoms in people after stroke.
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated in the abstract (objective to compare effectiveness on depressive symptoms after stroke).

elements.quote: The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review. 17 Participants (P): ... Interventions (I) and controls (C): This review considered trials that compared the effects of NPIs for post-stroke individuals with depressive symptoms (eg, music therapy, massage therapy, behavioral therapy, or physical exercise with any frequency, intensity, or duration) to control conditions, such as usual treatment.
elements.reason: For intervention-effect reviews, the planned comparisons are stated using an appropriate variant (PICOS), explicitly describing comparison of non-pharmacological interventions versus control conditions/usual treatment.

elements.quote: The search was restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) written in English and published in peer-reviewed journals. The PICOS (Participants, Interventions, Comparisons, Outcomes, Study Designs) checklist was used to identify the inclusion criteria in this review. 17 Participants (P): This review included trials if they targeted persons with stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic), regardless of comorbidities and any previous treatments, but excluded those with manic or psychotic episodes/symptoms in order to reduce biases associated with non-target symptoms. Participants were included whether or not they received pharmacological interventions (any dosage or duration) for depression or other illnesses. Interventions (I) and controls (C): This review considered trials that compared the effects of NPIs for post-stroke individuals with depressive symptoms (eg, music therapy, massage therapy, behavioral therapy, or physical exercise with any frequency, intensity, or duration) to control conditions, such as usual treatment. Outcomes (O): The primary outcome of this review was depressive symptoms, measured by any validated depression scale. Study designs (S): This review considered any RCT with a pre-post design, meaning that outcomes were measured at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and follow-up.
elements.reason: The eligibility criteria specify study characteristics using PICOS, including participants (stroke with exclusions), study design (RCT pre-post with follow-up), outcomes (depressive symptoms measured by validated depression scale), and the intervention/comparison structure for inclusion.

elements.quote: The search was restricted to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) written in English and published in peer-reviewed journals.
elements.reason: The review specifies report characteristics including language (English) and publication status (peer-reviewed journals).

elements.quote: Trials published between January 2000 and August 2018 were considered for inclusion; this date range reflects findings from an initial search in MEDLINE and CINAHL, which showed no relevant trials before 2000.
elements.reason: It provides a publication date range, but the evidence does not explicitly state inclusion criteria for dissemination year beyond this range, nor whether unpublished/other report statuses were considered.
No evidence is provided distinguishing exclusions because outcomes were not measured versus exclusions because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: These trials were grouped into four types: CAT (n = 5), exercise (n = 4), psychosocial therapy (n = 2), and multifactorial therapy (n = 2) (Table 2).
elements.reason: Groups used for synthesis are specified (CAT, exercise, psychosocial therapy, multifactorial therapy), but the evidence does not clearly show that each group is explicitly linked to comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: This review included trials if they targeted persons with stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic), regardless of comorbidities and any previous treatments, but excluded those with manic or psychotic episodes/symptoms in order to reduce biases associated with non-target symptoms.

Next, a second search using all identified interventions was performed across the following major online databases: Academic Search Complete; CINAHL Plus; MEDLINE; Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials; Scopus; and Library, Information Science and Technology Abstracts. Trials published between January 2000 and August 2018 were considered for inclusion;

elements.reason: Thresholds/ranges for interpreting effect size (0.2/0.5/0.8) and the rule for statistical significance based on 95% CI are reported.

elements.quote: We computed standardized mean differences (SMDs) based on between-group comparisons of pre-post (or follow-up) change in scores and pre-test SDs. In other words, this approach is a more consistent estimate of variance between groups.

elements.quote: The trials selected for potential inclusion were assessed for methodological rigor prior to inclusion by two reviewers using standardized critical appraisal instruments from the Joanna Briggs Institute Meta-Analysis of Statistics Assessment and Review Instrument (JBIMAStARI). 18 JBI-MAStARI is an analytic module in the JBI System for the Unified Management, Assessment and Review of Information package. Our reviewers established minimal requirements to qualify a study for inclusion in the review and progression to data extraction; inclusion required 'yes' answers to five mandatory questions on the JBIMAStARI standardized critical appraisal instrument. The five mandatory questions were Q5, Q6, Q8, Q9, and Q10.
elements.reason: The review describes the eligibility decision process for study inclusion in each synthesis, specifying that two reviewers used JBI-MAStARI and required 'yes' answers to specific mandatory questions (Q5, Q6, Q8, Q9, Q10) before inclusion and data extraction.

elements.quote: If the study reported the pre- and post-test means in each group, we obtained the changes by subtracting the post-test outcome from the pre-test outcome within each group. Where the pre-test SD was not available, we used the change in SDs. 22 In cases in which the study only reported standard errors (SEs), the SD was calculated using the following formula 23 : SD = SE × number of participants .
elements.reason: The review describes methods for preparing data for synthesis, including how change scores were calculated, how SDs were handled when pre-test SD was unavailable, and how SD was derived from reported SEs.
No description was retrieved about tabular structures used to display results of individual studies and syntheses or the data included within those tables.

elements.quote: Statistical analysis: We visually inspected the potential of publication bias by a funnel plot, examining asymmetry of the graph.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the graphical method used (funnel plot) and the visual inspection approach (asymmetry) for assessing publication bias.

elements.quote: These trials were grouped into four types: CAT (n = 5), exercise (n = 4), psychosocial therapy (n = 2), and multifactorial therapy (n = 2) (Table 2).
elements.reason: The basis for grouping studies into categories (types of interventions) is reported, but the retrieved evidence does not explicitly explain the ordering/grouping rules for all tables/graphs beyond this categorization.
No rationale for using any non-standard graphs was retrieved.

elements.quote: For the meta-analysis, we calculated effect sizes and statistical heterogeneity using Review Manager (RevMan) 5.3 software (Nordic Cochrane Centre, Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen 2014).
elements.reason: The software package (Review Manager/RevMan) and version number (5.3) used for statistical synthesis are reported.
The evidence describes meta-analysis methods being performed; no statement indicates an alternative synthesis method was used because meta-analysis was impossible.

elements.quote: We applied the random effect model in all calculations of effect size because all included trials had variations in study design, intervention methods, and population characteristics.
elements.reason: The random-effects model is used and the rationale for choosing it is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity test: We applied the random effect model in all calculations of effect size... The Chi-square test (Cochran's Q) and I 2 statistics were used to identify heterogeneity among the included trials.
elements.reason: The evidence specifies the random-effects approach and heterogeneity assessment (Cochran’s Q and I²), but it does not clearly specify the exact statistical method used for the random-effects meta-analysis (e.g., the specific estimator/procedure).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity test: We applied the random effect model... The Chi-square test (Cochran's Q) and I 2 statistics were used to identify heterogeneity among the included trials. Heterogeneity was present if the Q value was significant (p < 0.10). I 2 statistics represent the degree of heterogeneity...
elements.reason: The methods to identify/quantify statistical heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q and I²), including the decision rule (Q significance threshold) and interpretation of I² are described.
No between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Calculation of effect size: To obtain effect sizes, SMDs and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cohen's d test in which the pooled effect estimate (ie, depressive symptoms) was assessed using various measurements.
elements.reason: The evidence states that 95% CIs were estimated and indicates the approach (Cohen's d test) used when obtaining SMDs and the corresponding 95% CIs.
No additional random-effects implementation details beyond applying a random-effects model and heterogeneity testing are provided in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence reports a (frequentist) random-effects model, and no Bayesian meta-analysis is described.
There is no description of methods to handle statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study.
The evidence does not identify any planned syntheses judged impossible or inappropriate, nor provide reasons for not performing specific syntheses.

elements.quote: Due to low heterogeneity, we did not run meta-regression analyses to understand the cause of heterogeneity. 33

elements.quote:
These identified interventions appear to be similar to interventions described in previous systematic reviews. 8,11,14 Yet, to the best of our knowledge, none of the previous reviews have applied meta-analyses to pool information on different intervention types; this is the first meta-analysis study quantifying the effectiveness of NPIs and comparing the impact of each intervention type on depressive symptoms after stroke.

Our study is consistent with previous strokespecific reviews that have qualitatively supported the effect of NPIs in reducing the severity of depressive symptoms. 8,11,13

Small effects are commonly found in reviews examining the effect of behavioral treatments on depression in other adult populations, especially reviews that only include high-quality studies. 37,38

Previous reviews have shown positive effects of music therapy on depressive symptoms in other populations, such as people with cancer 40 and dementia. 41 A recent review reported a similar positive effect of music therapy on mood in neurological populations. 42

These findings are incongruent with two earlier reviews. The first review, conducted in 2000, reported that research on psychosocial therapy for post-stroke depression remains unsophisticated and has methodological limitations to establishment of its effects. 47 The second review, conducted in 2008, revealed no effect of psychosocial therapy for the treatment of post-stroke depression. 6

Aligning with this explanation, our findings concur with results from a recent review performed in 2013. 48

It is possible that NPIs may have a small effect size per se, as small effect sizes are also reported in other psychological interventions for depression in general. 31,32
elements.reason: In the Discussion, the authors interpret their findings by comparing them with results from prior systematic reviews and other evidence, including consistency/inconsistency with earlier reviews and explanations in the context of existing literature.

elements.quote: This review provides meaningful evidence in clinical research and practice; however, it has a few limitations resulting from the research design of the included trials. First, the majority of the included trials narrowed their selection criteria to people without communication problems/aphasia, cognitive impairments, and other neurological or psychiatric disorders. Considering the high prevalence of aphasia, cognitive impairments, and/or other comorbid conditions among people after stroke, this narrow selection criteria may cause study bias and limit the generalizability of study findings. ... Second, study characteristics, such as the number of intervention sessions, interventions for the control conditions, and the stage of stroke recovery, varied across all included studies. ... This review attempted to group many disparate and diverse therapeutic interventions into one category of NPI. ... Last, the number of trials used to test the effects of specific intervention types may be inadequate. The interpretation of these study results should be cautious.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly discusses limitations of the included trials/evidence (e.g., narrow eligibility criteria affecting generalizability, variability in study characteristics increasing heterogeneity, grouping diverse interventions, and inadequate number of trials), fulfilling the criterion to discuss limitations of the evidence included.
